about: The Party match questionnaire (/match). Each question points at a row of the Compare matrix (components/compare/model.ts matrixRows), so every list's answer, shade and basis come from data/positions and data/comparison-questions.json. Options are the reader's version of a row's stances; a stance with no option (a historical record or a split) still places its lists. Spec: docs/planning/2026-10-08-match/SPEC.md.

core.prompt: Should Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) yeshiva students be drafted into the army?
core.context: Most Israeli Jews are conscripted at 18. Haredi men in full-time religious study have largely been exempt since 1948, and the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the exemption has no legal basis.

options.no-compulsion: No one should be compelled to serve
options.exempt-learners: Exempt those who study Torah full time
options.draft-leavers: Draft only those who leave yeshiva
options.expand-gradually: Raise Haredi service step by step
options.draft-all: Everyone serves, in the army or a civilian service

core.prompt: Should power shift from the courts to the Knesset and the government?
core.context: Israel has no written constitution. Its Supreme Court can strike down laws and government decisions, and the 2023 judicial overhaul, which set out to curb it, brought months of mass protest.

options.curb: Yes, curb the Supreme Court's powers
options.limited-override: Let the Knesset override the court in limited cases
options.codify: Settle the balance in a Basic Law, a kind of constitution

core.prompt: Who should investigate the failures of October 7?
core.context: Israel's 1968 law sets up a state commission of inquiry whose members are chosen by the president of the Supreme Court. The government has proposed a different commission whose members the court would not choose.

options.other-commission: A commission set up outside the 1968 law
options.independent-unset: An independent inquiry; the exact form can wait
options.state-commission: A state commission of inquiry under the 1968 law

core.prompt: Should Israel annex land in the occupied West Bank?
core.context: Israel has held the West Bank since 1967 without annexing it. About half a million Israeli settlers and some three million Palestinians live there. Annexation would apply Israeli law to the land.

options.annex-part: Annex Area C or chosen areas
options.sovereignty-not-bills: Back sovereignty in principle, but not by law now
options.no-annexation: No annexation; work toward a Palestinian state

core.prompt: Should there be a Palestinian state?
core.context: A Palestinian state beside Israel has been the aim of most international peace plans since the 1990s. Most lists running in 2026 oppose one; a few support it.

options.not-on-agenda: Not now; it is not on the agenda
options.separation: Separation as part of a regional deal

core.prompt: Who should run marriage, conversion and the rules for Shabbat?
core.context: Israel has no civil marriage: Jews marry through the Orthodox Chief Rabbinate, and many couples marry abroad instead. The rabbinate also controls conversion, and Shabbat rules such as public transport are set nationally.

options.civil-local: Allow civil marriage, and let towns set Shabbat rules
options.civil-pluralist: Allow civil marriage and recognise non-Orthodox conversion

core.prompt: What should economic policy put first?
core.context: The cost of living is among Israelis' top worries. The lists' economic priorities can coexist rather than run from one end to another, so the match here is on the priority you put first.

options.market: Free markets and a smaller state
options.living-costs: Lower living costs and narrower gaps
options.reward-service: Rewarding those who serve in the army or reserves
options.own-community: Budgets for communities that have been left behind

deeper.prompt: Should young Haredi men who have left yeshiva be required to serve?
deeper.context: Even some lists that defend the exemption for full-time students disagree over men who are no longer studying.

deeper.prompt: In a service framework, military or civilian, who should be exempt?
deeper.context: The draft plans differ most on who would still be exempt.

options.none: No one: no exemptions or quotas
options.outstanding: A small number of outstanding scholars
options.learners: Everyone studying in yeshiva full time

deeper.prompt: Should the 2025 law that gave politicians more say in choosing judges be repealed?
deeper.context: The March 2025 law replaced the Israel Bar Association's two seats on the committee that selects judges with public representatives chosen by the coalition and the opposition. It takes effect in the next Knesset.

deeper.prompt: Should the Knesset be able to pass again a law the Supreme Court has struck down?
deeper.context: An "override clause" was the most contested part of the 2023 overhaul. The answers differ on how large a majority it would need.

options.61: Yes, with a simple majority of 61
options.supermajority: Only with a special majority, 70 MKs or more

deeper.prompt: Should the courts keep "reasonableness" as grounds to overturn government decisions?
deeper.context: In 2023 the Knesset abolished the standard for decisions by the cabinet and ministers; the Supreme Court struck that law down in 2024.

options.abolish: Abolish it for decisions by the cabinet and ministers

deeper.prompt: Should couples be able to marry in a civil ceremony inside Israel?
deeper.context: Today a civil marriage performed abroad is registered in Israel, but none can be performed in the country.

deeper.prompt: Should towns be able to run public transport on Shabbat?
deeper.context: Most buses and trains stop from Friday evening to Saturday evening. A few cities run limited services of their own.

options.keep: No, keep the current Shabbat rules

deeper.prompt: Should Israel recognise conversions to Judaism done outside the Orthodox establishment?
deeper.context: Recognition decides who is Jewish under Israeli law for marriage and burial, which matters to many Reform and Conservative Jews.
